question: An operator sets aerodrome operating minima. What limit applies to them?

options.text: Not lower than the regulatory values or the State's
Whatever the chief pilot considers safe for each crew
Exactly the values on the approach chart
Not higher than the State's published values

explanation: Minima must not be lower than the values in the regulations, the method must be acceptable to the authority, and they must not be lower than minima set by the aerodrome's State unless that State approves.

question: Which equipment may allow operations below the normal aerodrome operating minima?

options.text: HUD, HUD landing system or enhanced vision system
An extra VHF radio and a second transponder with Mode S

explanation: The use of a head-up display, head-up display landing system or enhanced vision system may allow operations at lower visibilities than normally associated with the operating minima.

question: May minima be calculated in flight for an alternate that was not planned?

options.text: Only by the dispatcher on the ground
Only for aerodromes with CAT III

explanation: In-flight calculation of minima for a non-planned alternate is allowed if carried out in accordance with an accepted method.

question: Which of these must the operator take into account when setting operating minima?

options.text: The time since the aeroplane was last washed and inspected
The crew's composition, competence and experience

explanation: Factors include the aeroplane's type, performance and handling; crew composition, competence and experience; runway dimensions; ground aids; aircraft equipment; obstacles; OCA/OCH; met reporting; and the final approach technique.

question: Unless approved otherwise, how must all approaches be flown?

options.text: At the maximum permitted speed until 1000 ft

explanation: All approaches shall be flown as stabilised approaches unless otherwise approved for a particular approach to a particular runway.

question: Unless approved otherwise, which technique must be used on non-precision approaches?

options.text: A visual circuit from the final approach fix
Level flight at MDA to the missed approach point

explanation: All non-precision approaches shall be flown with the CDFA technique unless otherwise approved for a particular approach and runway.

question: On what is the aeroplane approach category based?

options.text: The indicated airspeed at threshold, VAT

explanation: Aeroplane categories are based on VAT, the indicated airspeed at the threshold, at maximum certified landing mass.

question: How is VAT calculated?

options.text: VS0 × 1.3 or VS1g × 1.23, at max landing mass

explanation: VAT equals the stall speed in the landing configuration (VS0) × 1.3, or the 1g stall speed (VS1g) × 1.23, at maximum certified landing mass. If both are available, the higher VAT is used.

question: Both VS0 and VS1g are available. Which VAT is used?

options.text: The lower of the two results
The higher of the two results
The one based on VS0, always

explanation: If VS0 and VS1g are both available, the higher resulting VAT is used.

question: Which category is an aeroplane with VAT of 135 kt?
explanation: Category C covers VAT from 121 to 140 kt. B is 91–120 kt and D is 141–165 kt.

question: What VAT range defines Category A?
explanation: Category A is VAT less than 91 kt.

question: What VAT range defines Category D?
explanation: Category D is VAT from 141 to 165 kt. Category E is 166 to 210 kt.

question: An aeroplane has VS0 of 100 kt at maximum landing mass. What is its category?
explanation: VAT = 100 × 1.3 = 130 kt, which falls in Category C (121–140 kt).

question: Which of these is a low visibility operation?

options.text: An autocoupled approach with autoland and auto roll-out
A non-precision approach flown in good visibility by day

explanation: Low visibility operations include manual take-off, autocoupled approach to below DH with manual landing, autoland with manual roll-out, autoland with auto roll-out when RVR is below 400 m, and approaches with HUDLS or EVS.

question: In low visibility operations, where should crew duties allow the commander to concentrate?

options.text: On flying the aircraft by hand

explanation: Duties must be distributed so the pilot deciding whether to land or go around can devote himself mainly to supervision and decision making.

question: Below what height must all height calls in low visibility operations be based on the radio altimeter?
explanation: All height calls below 200 ft must be based on the radio altimeter, and one pilot must continue to monitor the instruments until landing is complete.

question: Which of these is a condition for Category II and III operations?

options.text: A crew of at least three pilots
An aircraft less than 10 years old
A crew of at least two pilots

explanation: CAT II/III needs aircraft certificated for DH below 200 ft (or no DH), a system for recording approach and autoland success and failure, authority approval, at least two pilots, and DH determined by radio altimeter.

question: How is decision height determined for Category II and III operations?
explanation: For CAT II/III, DH is determined by a radio altimeter.

question: Below what RVR does a take-off need authority approval for Category A, B and C aeroplanes?
explanation: An operator shall not conduct low visibility take-offs in less than 150 m RVR for Category A, B and C aeroplanes, or 200 m for Category D, unless approved.

question: What is circling?

options.text: The visual part of an approach, to land on another runway
A go-around flown visually after a missed approach
An orbit given by ATC for spacing
A holding pattern flown at the final approach fix

explanation: Circling is the visual phase of an instrument approach to bring an aeroplane into position to land on a runway not suitably located for a straight-in approach.

question: What is a low visibility take-off (LVTO)?

options.text: A take-off with RVR below 400 m
A take-off with visibility below 5 km
A take-off with RVR below 800 m

explanation: In these rules, a low visibility take-off is a take-off where the RVR is less than 400 m.

question: What is a fail-passive flight control system?

options.text: After a failure the landing is still completed automatically
A system that the pilot must monitor only below 50 ft
No significant deviation, but no automatic landing

explanation: A fail-passive system has no significant out-of-trim or flight path deviation after a failure, but the landing is not completed automatically; the pilot takes control.

question: What is a fail-operational flight control system?

options.text: A system that disconnects at the first failure
A system used only for take-off guidance
After a failure the pilot must take control at once
Automatic landing still completed after a failure

explanation: A fail-operational system can complete the approach, flare and landing automatically after a failure below alert height; it then works as a fail-passive system.

question: What is a fail-operational hybrid landing system?

options.text: An autoland with no pilot monitoring
Fail-passive autoland plus independent manual guidance
A head-up display with no autopilot

explanation: It consists of a primary fail-passive automatic landing system and a secondary independent guidance system allowing the pilot to land manually after a primary failure.

question: What is a visual approach?

options.text: Any approach flown in VMC under VFR
An approach to a runway with no instrument procedure

explanation: A visual approach is one where part or all of an instrument procedure is not completed and the approach is flown with visual reference to terrain.

question: To what point is a CDFA flown?

options.text: About 50 ft above the threshold, or where the flare begins
The MDA, then level flight to the missed approach point at MDA
The runway touchdown point at 3° exactly

explanation: CDFA is a continuous descent, without level-off, from at or above the FAF altitude to about 15 m (50 ft) above the threshold or the point where the flare begins.

question: What is a stabilised approach?

options.text: An approach at a constant speed of VREF + 20
One flown with controlled energy and path to 50 ft

explanation: A stabilised approach is flown in a controlled and appropriate manner in terms of configuration, energy and flight path control from a predetermined point down to 50 ft above the threshold or the flare point if higher.

question: What is a head-up display (HUD)?

options.text: A display mounted on the pilot's helmet only
A screen in the centre console
A display showing only engine data
Flight data shown in the pilot's forward view

explanation: A HUD presents flight information in the pilot's forward external field of view without significantly restricting the outside view.

question: A head-up display landing system (HUDLS) is typically used for primary guidance down to what decision height?
explanation: A HUDLS is typically used for primary approach guidance to decision heights of 50 ft.

question: What is an enhanced vision system (EVS)?

options.text: A real-time sensor image of the scene ahead
A brighter set of landing lights
Spectacles that improve the pilot's eyesight
A camera that records the flight for training

explanation: EVS is an electronic means of displaying a real-time image of the external scene using imaging sensors.

question: How are take-off minima expressed?

options.text: As visibility or RVR (plus ceiling if needed)
As the DH for the departure runway

explanation: Take-off minima are visibility or RVR limits; where obstacles must be seen and avoided or a forced landing considered, further conditions such as a ceiling are specified.

question: When may the commander take off if the departure weather is below landing minima for that aerodrome?

options.text: Whenever the take-off minima are met
Only if a suitable take-off alternate is available

explanation: The commander shall not take off unless the departure weather is at or above landing minima for that aerodrome, unless a suitable take-off alternate is available.

question: No RVR or visibility is reported at the departure aerodrome. When may the take-off start?

options.text: When the previous aircraft took off without problems
When he can confirm the runway visibility is enough

explanation: When no visibility or RVR is reported, the take-off may only start if the commander can determine that the RVR/visibility along the runway is at or above the required minimum.

question: Take-off minima must give enough visual guidance for which situations?

options.text: A return to land immediately after take-off
A take-off with all engines working only
Taxiing to the runway in fog
A rejected or continued take-off after engine failure

explanation: Take-off minima must ensure sufficient guidance to control the aeroplane in a discontinued take-off in adverse circumstances and in a continued take-off after failure of the critical engine.

question: With no runway lighting or markings, by day only, what is the minimum take-off RVR or visibility?
explanation: With nil facilities, by day only, the minimum is 500 m.

question: With runway edge lighting and/or centre line marking, what is the take-off RVR for Category A, B and C aeroplanes?
explanation: With edge lighting and/or centre line marking the minimum is 250 m, or 300 m for Category D.

question: With runway edge and centre line lighting, what is the take-off RVR for Category D aeroplanes?
explanation: With edge and centre line lighting the minimum is 200 m for Category A, B and C, and 250 m for Category D.

question: With edge and centre line lighting plus multiple RVR information, what is the take-off RVR for Category A, B and C?
explanation: With edge and centre line lighting and multiple RVR information the minimum is 150 m (200 m for Category D), achieved at all relevant reporting points.

question: For night take-offs, what minimum runway lighting is required?

options.text: Runway edge and runway end lights
No lights, if the aircraft has landing lights

explanation: For night operations at least runway edge and runway end lights are required.

question: What may replace the reported RVR for the initial part of the take-off run?

options.text: The RVR from the stop end
The ATIS visibility from the previous hour
The visibility reported at the nearest other aerodrome

explanation: The reported RVR/visibility for the initial part of the take-off run can be replaced by pilot assessment.

question: An aeroplane cannot meet the engine-failure performance conditions. On what are its take-off minima based?

options.text: The aerodrome's highest obstacle within 1 NM
The height from which the net flight path can be built
The length of the runway only

explanation: For such aeroplanes the take-off minima are based on the height from which the one-engine-inoperative net take-off flight path can be constructed, which decides the RVR needed to see and avoid obstacles or re-land.

question: If an engine failure is assumed between 101 and 150 ft, what take-off RVR is required?
explanation: The table gives: below 50 ft 200 m; 51–100 ft 300 m; 101–150 ft 400 m; 151–200 ft 500 m; 201–300 ft 1000 m; above 300 ft 1500 m.

question: If an engine failure is assumed above 300 ft, or no positive flight path can be constructed, what RVR is required?
explanation: Above 300 ft, or if no positive take-off flight path can be constructed, the take-off RVR/visibility is 1500 m.

question: With approval, to what RVR may take-off minima be reduced for Category A, B and C aeroplanes?
explanation: With approval, take-off minima may be reduced to 125 m RVR (150 m for Category D) under specific conditions.

question: Which of these is a condition for a take-off at 125 m RVR?

options.text: A 90 m visual segment at the start of the run
A visibility of 400 m at the stop end

explanation: Conditions are: LVP in force, high-intensity centre line lights at 15 m or less and edge lights at 60 m or less, simulator training, a 90 m visual segment from the flight deck at the start of the run, and the RVR achieved at all relevant points.

question: For a 125 m RVR take-off, what is the maximum spacing of high-intensity runway centre line lights?
explanation: High-intensity centre line lights must be spaced at 15 m or less and edge lights at 60 m or less.

question: With an approved lateral guidance system or HUD, what is the lowest take-off RVR allowed?
explanation: With an approved lateral guidance system or HUD/HUDLS, take-off minima may be reduced below 125 m (150 m for Cat D) but not below 75 m, given CAT III-equivalent runway protection and facilities.

question: Who must approve an aerodrome for Category II and III operations?

options.text: The State in which the aerodrome is situated

explanation: An operator shall not use an aerodrome for CAT II/III unless it is approved for such operations by the State in which it is located, and must verify that LVPs are established and enforced.

question: Before conducting CAT II/III, what training must flight crew complete?

options.text: Simulator training and checks to the limiting values
Only line training on the aircraft
Nothing extra if they hold a type rating

explanation: Each flight crew member completes prescribed training and checking, including simulator training to the limiting RVR and DH of the operator's approval, under an approved training programme. This is in addition to other training.

question: Before starting a CAT II/III approach, what must the commander confirm with ATC?

options.text: That the fire service has been alerted
That low visibility procedures are in force
That no other aircraft are on approach

explanation: The commander must be satisfied, from ATC information, that appropriate low visibility procedures are in force before starting a low visibility take-off or CAT II/III approach.

question: Where must the minimum equipment for low visibility operations be listed?
explanation: The operations manual must contain the minimum equipment that must be serviceable before low visibility operations can start.

question: What are system minima?

options.text: The minima published by the State
The lowest DH or MDH the equipment allows
The operator's minima for a new captain

explanation: System minima are heights derived for the lowest permitted DH or MDH considering the characteristics of the ground and airborne equipment.

question: What is the lowest MDH for a localiser-only approach?
explanation: Localiser with or without DME: 250 ft.

question: What is the lowest MDH for an NDB approach?
explanation: NDB: 350 ft. NDB/DME: 300 ft.

question: What is the lowest MDH for a VOR approach without DME?
explanation: VOR: 300 ft; VOR/DME: 250 ft.

question: What is the lowest MDH for a VOR/DME approach?
explanation: VOR/DME: 250 ft.

question: What is the lowest MDH for a surveillance radar approach terminating at 2 NM?
explanation: SRA terminating at 0.5 NM: 250 ft; at 1 NM: 300 ft; at 2 NM: 350 ft.

question: What is the lowest MDH for a VDF (QDM/QGH) approach?
explanation: VDF (QDM and QGH): 350 ft.

question: What is the lowest MDH for an RNAV/LNAV approach?
explanation: RNAV/LNAV: 300 ft.

question: The MDH for a non-precision approach must not be lower than which values?

options.text: The category OCH and the system minimum
The circling MDH for the category

explanation: The MDH must not be lower than either the OCH for the aeroplane category or the system minimum.

question: When is MDH measured from the threshold rather than the aerodrome elevation?

options.text: When the threshold is above the aerodrome elevation
When the runway is longer than 3000 m
When the threshold is 2 m or more below aerodrome level

explanation: MDH is normally based on aerodrome elevation; if the threshold elevation is 2 m or more below aerodrome elevation, MDH is measured from the threshold.

question: Which of these is an acceptable visual reference to continue below MDA/H?
explanation: At least one of: approach lights, threshold, threshold markings or lights, threshold identification lights, visual glide slope indicator, touchdown zone or its markings or lights, runway edge lights, or other accepted references.

question: What minimum MDH and RVR define a non-precision approach operation in these rules?

options.text: MDH not below 200 ft and RVR not below 550 m
MDH not below 250 ft and RVR not below 750 m
MDH not below 300 ft and RVR not below 1000 m
MDH not below 350 ft and RVR not below 800 m

explanation: An NPA operation has an MDH or DH not lower than 250 ft and RVR/CMV not less than 750 m, unless accepted otherwise.

question: What is an APV operation?

options.text: A precision approach with an autoland
Lateral and vertical guidance, below precision standard
An approach with lateral guidance only

explanation: An APV operation uses lateral and vertical guidance but does not meet the precision approach requirements, with DH not below 250 ft and RVR not below 600 m unless approved.

question: What are the lowest DH and RVR for an APV operation, unless approved otherwise?
explanation: APV: DH not lower than 250 ft and RVR not less than 600 m unless approved.

question: Which aids may be used for a Category I precision approach?
explanation: A CAT I operation is a precision approach and landing using ILS, MLS, GLS (GNSS/GBAS) or PAR.

question: What is the lowest RVR for a standard Category I approach?
explanation: CAT I needs RVR not less than 550 m unless accepted. Lower-than-standard CAT I, when authorised, may go down to 400 m depending on lighting.

question: What is the lowest decision height for a Category I approach?
explanation: The CAT I DH must not be lower than the flight manual minimum, the minimum height the aid can be used without visual reference, the OCH, or 200 ft.

question: Required RVR can be found from the formula RVR = (DH × 0.3048 / tan α) − approach light length. What is α by default?
explanation: α is the calculation angle, by default 3°, increasing in steps.

question: Using the formula with a 3° angle, what RVR results from DH 200 ft with 720 m of approach lights?

options.text: About 440 m (then subject to the 550 m minimum)
About 1160 m, before deducting the approach light length

explanation: 200 × 0.3048 = 61 m; 61 / tan 3° = 61 / 0.0524 ≈ 1163 m; minus 720 m ≈ 443 m. The standard CAT I minimum of 550 m still applies unless lower-than-standard CAT I is authorised.

question: What is the minimum RVR for single-pilot operations, unless a coupled autopilot or approved HUDLS is used?
explanation: For single-pilot operations the minimum RVR is 800 m, except when using a suitable autopilot coupled to an ILS or MLS, or an approved HUDLS, when normal minima apply.

question: What decision height defines a Category II operation?

options.text: Below 200 ft but not lower than 100 ft
Below 250 ft but not lower than 200 ft

explanation: CAT II uses ILS or MLS with DH below 200 ft but not lower than 100 ft and RVR not less than 300 m.

question: What is the lowest RVR for a Category II operation?
explanation: CAT II requires RVR of not less than 300 m.

question: What visual reference is needed to continue below a Category II DH?

options.text: The touchdown zone lights only, with no lateral element
Three consecutive lights plus a lateral element

explanation: A segment of at least 3 consecutive lights (approach centre line, TDZ, runway centre line or edge lights, or a combination) must be seen, including a lateral element such as an approach crossbar, the threshold or a TDZ barrette, unless using an approved HUDLS to touchdown.

question: For a Category II approach with DH 100–120 ft, what RVR applies to Category A, B and C aeroplanes?
explanation: DH 100–120 ft: 300 m (Category D 350 m, or 300 m with autoland). DH 121–140 ft: 400 m. DH 141 ft and above: 450 m.

question: For a Category II approach with DH 130 ft, what RVR applies?
explanation: DH 121–140 ft requires 400 m RVR.

question: A Category D aeroplane flies a CAT II approach with DH 110 ft, without autoland. What RVR applies?
explanation: For DH 100–120 ft, Category D needs 350 m, unless conducting an autoland, when 300 m may be used.

question: In the CAT II table, what does "autocoupled to below DH" mean?

options.text: The autopilot is used down to the DH exactly
The autopilot is used only above 1000 ft
Autopilot used down to 80% of the DH or below
The approach is flown by hand with flight director

explanation: It means continued use of the automatic flight control system down to a height not greater than 80% of the applicable DH.

question: How is a Category IIIA operation defined?

options.text: DH below 200 ft and RVR not less than 300 m
No DH and no RVR limit
DH below 50 ft and RVR below 175 m
DH below 100 ft and RVR not less than 175 m

explanation: By definition, CAT IIIA has a DH lower than 100 ft and an RVR not less than 175 m. Operator minima tables may set a higher figure, such as 200 m.

question: How is a Category IIIB operation defined?

options.text: DH below 50 ft or none; RVR 50 m to below 175 m
DH below 100 ft and RVR not less than 175 m
DH below 200 ft and RVR not less than 300 m
No DH and no RVR requirement

explanation: By definition, CAT IIIB has a DH lower than 50 ft or no DH, and an RVR lower than 175 m but not less than 50 m. Operator minima tables commonly go no lower than 75 m.

question: What defines a Category IIIC operation?

options.text: DH below 100 ft and RVR at least 175 m
DH below 50 ft and RVR at least 75 m
No DH and no RVR requirement
No DH and RVR at least 50 m

explanation: CAT IIIC: no decision height and no runway visual range limitations.

question: The DH and the RVR of an approach fall into different categories. Which decides the category?

options.text: The lower of the two categories

explanation: Where DH and RVR do not fall within the same category, the RVR determines the category of the operation.

question: Which of these is a condition for operations with no decision height?

options.text: The runway is longer than 3000 m
The flight manual authorises no-DH operations
The crew has at least three pilots

explanation: No-DH operations require authorisation in the flight manual, approach aid and aerodrome facilities that support them, and an operator approval for CAT III with no DH.

question: For CAT IIIA or IIIB with a fail-passive system, what visual reference is needed below DH?
explanation: With fail-passive systems or an approved HUDLS, a segment of at least 3 consecutive lights must be attained and maintained.

question: For CAT IIIB with a fail-operational system and a DH, what visual reference is needed?

options.text: A lateral element of the lighting
At least one centre line light

explanation: For CAT IIIB with fail-operational systems using a DH, at least one centre line light must be attained and maintained.

question: For CAT III with no decision height, what visual reference is required before touchdown?

options.text: At least one centre line light

explanation: For Category III operations with no DH there is no requirement for visual contact with the runway before touchdown.

question: In the operator minima table, what is the lowest RVR for CAT IIIA (DH below 100 ft, no roll-out system required)?
explanation: The operator minima table gives 200 m for CAT IIIA, above the 175 m that defines the category.

question: For CAT IIIB with DH below 100 ft and a fail-passive roll-out system, what is the lowest RVR?
explanation: IIIB, DH below 100 ft, fail-passive roll-out: 150 m. DH below 50 ft, fail-passive: 125 m. DH below 50 ft or no DH, fail-operational: 75 m.

question: For CAT IIIB with DH below 50 ft or no DH and a fail-operational roll-out system, what is the lowest RVR?
explanation: With a fail-operational roll-out control or guidance system and DH below 50 ft or no DH, the lowest RVR is 75 m.

question: During a circling approach, what height is maintained until established on visual final?
explanation: The instrument approach terminates at the circling MDH, which is maintained during the circling manoeuvre until established on visual final for the landing runway.

question: What are the circling MDH and visibility for a Category C aeroplane?
explanation: Circling minima: Cat A 400 ft/1500 m; Cat B 500 ft/1600 m; Cat C 600 ft/2400 m; Cat D 700 ft/3600 m.

question: What are the circling MDH and visibility for a Category D aeroplane?
explanation: Category D: MDH 700 ft and visibility 3600 m.

question: What are the circling MDH and visibility for a Category A aeroplane?
explanation: Category A: MDH 400 ft and visibility 1500 m.

question: Below what RVR may an operator not conduct a visual approach?
explanation: An operator is not to conduct visual approaches when the RVR is less than 800 m.

question: At the start of a visual approach, must the pilot see the landing runway?

options.text: No, but he must navigate by terrain
Only if the cloud base is below 1000 ft

explanation: There is no requirement to see the aerodrome or runway at the start, but the pilot must be able to navigate with reference to the terrain.

question: For a VFR flight above 3000 ft AMSL in Class C airspace, what distance from cloud is required?

options.text: Clear of cloud and in sight of the surface

explanation: Above 900 m (3000 ft) AMSL or 300 m (1000 ft) above terrain, whichever is higher, VMC requires 1500 m horizontally and 300 m (1000 ft) vertically from cloud.

question: At and above 10 000 ft AMSL, what flight visibility does VMC require?
explanation: Flight visibility must be 8 km at and above 3050 m (10 000 ft) AMSL, and 5 km below.

question: When the transition altitude is below 10 000 ft, what level replaces 10 000 ft for the VMC visibility change?
explanation: When the transition altitude is lower than 10 000 ft, FL100 is used instead of 10 000 ft.

question: In Class F or G airspace at or below 3000 ft AMSL (or 1000 ft above terrain), what cloud clearance is needed?

options.text: Clear of cloud and in sight of the surface

explanation: At and below 900 m (3000 ft) AMSL or 300 m (1000 ft) above terrain in Class F and G, the aircraft must be clear of cloud and in sight of the surface.

question: In uncontrolled airspace at low level, when may Category A and B aeroplanes fly with a visibility down to 3000 m?

options.text: If the pilot holds an instrument rating
If ATS permits, traffic is light and IAS ≤ 140 kt

explanation: Category A and B aeroplanes may use flight visibilities down to 3000 m if the ATS authority permits, the probability of meeting other traffic is low and the IAS is 140 kt or less.

question: Below what visibility may a special VFR flight not be started?
explanation: Special VFR flights are not to be started when the visibility (flight or ground) is less than 3 km.

question: Below what flight visibility may a special VFR flight not continue?
explanation: A special VFR flight is not to be continued when the flight visibility is less than 1.5 km.
